papers.title: Walrus Technical Report
papers.abstract: We present Walrus, a unified 8B speech-and-audio foundation model handling speech recognition (including code-switching and multi-talker speech), speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation, text-to-speech, emotion recognition, audio captioning, and general audio understanding. Our main contribution is not a new architecture but a data-centric training recipe; we use a standard decoder-only backbone initialized from Gemma 4, so that gains can be traced to the data. For speech generation, Walrus predicts low-bitrate discrete speech tokens, and a lightweight token-to-waveform decoder converts them into high-fidelity audio. The recipe is a three-stage data curriculum that moves from broad multilingual data to multi-talker, code-switching, and domain-specific data. At each stage, task-aware and dataset-aware weighting balances tasks with very different token budgets and protects core skills from forgetting. Trained on over 600M samples covering more than 20 tasks and 100 languages, Walrus leads on most multilingual, multi-talker, and code-switching ASR, speech translation, and audio understanding benchmarks, outperforming both open speech language models of comparable size and dedicated task-specific models. On most benchmarks, it even matches or surpasses the $4\times$ larger Qwen3-Omni's performance. Results suggest that data engineering is a primary driver of quality in multi-task speech and audio modeling.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech generation, text-to-speech, speech translation
Audio & Speech Language Models: speech language model, audio foundation model
Audio Understanding & Reasoning: audio captioning, audio understanding

papers.title: Alania-2: Turkish text-to-speech with instant and fine-tuned voice cloning
papers.abstract: We present Alania-2, a Turkish text-to-speech (TTS) system with two built-in voices, voice design from text descriptions, and two kinds of voice cloning. Alania-2 is a 488M-parameter model with the VoxCPM architecture, which generates continuous audio latents with a diffusion head on top of a language-model backbone. We train it from scratch on 18,195 hours of Turkish speech, 90% of which is synthetic speech produced by a larger teacher model and filtered automatically. A text normalizer rewrites numbers, abbreviations and foreign names into the words a Turkish speaker would say; without it, none of 96 test sentences with digits kept all its critical parts, such as an amount or a date, through synthesis and speech recognition, against 86 with it. On Freya-TR-Eval, a public benchmark of 495 Turkish sentences scored with automatic speech recognition, Alania-2 reaches a word error rate of 1.44%, compared with 5.99% for our previous system. On its built-in voices, it comes within half a point of character error rate of a 2.3B-parameter model at under a quarter of the size, and a 7.6M-parameter single-voice model trained with the same recipe matches the most intelligible systems we measured, which suggests that training data matters more for intelligibility than model size. We also report practical findings on voice cloning: conditioning on the reference audio alone, rather than continuing it, cuts skipped words from 21.9% to 1.7%; 20-30 seconds of reference audio works best; and a low-rank adapter trained in about two minutes raises speaker similarity well above instant cloning. Finally, we describe inference-engine changes that bring first audio down to 32 ms for a single stream. We release our evaluation harness and three Turkish speech and text datasets.
papers.venue: 21 pages, 11 figures, 10 tables. Evaluation harness and results: https://huggingface.co/datasets/PatientdeskAI/freya-tr-eval-rerun
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: text-to-speech, automatic speech recognition, voice cloning

papers.title: MusicFlux: Flexible Conditioning for Text-Guided Music Generation and Editing
papers.abstract: Music editing transforms existing recordings while preserving their original attributes. Recent approaches adapt pretrained text-to-music models for tasks like inpainting, event insertion, or restoration by conditioning them with context audio. It was recently proposed for image editing to unify generation and editing by treating the source image as in-context information. However, applying this directly to music is computationally expensive due to long audio sequences. In this work, we develop MusicFlux, a text-guided music editor built on an efficient pretrained flow-matching text-to-audio model. We introduce two conditioning approaches that trade off editing performance and computational efficiency. Experiments show that both are competitive with strong baselines, with one achieving better editing quality and the other preserving the original sequence length and substantially improving computational efficiency.
authors: Leonardo Boulitreau de Menezes Martins Marques
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: text-to-music, music generation, text-to-audio

papers.title: Nepali-English Code-Mixed Speech Recognition: Data Preparation and Adaptation of a Speech Foundation Model
papers.abstract: Nepali speakers regularly mix English words into conversation, but multilingual speech recognisers often struggle with language switches and the writing script used for English words. We study how to adapt SraVaani, a 449M-parameter hybrid TDT-CTC model, using a 172.8-hour corpus covering six Nepali speech domains. Its pretrained tokenizer does not support digits and several common symbols. Rather than replace it or discard these recordings, we generate Nepali and English readings for numbers and use zero-shot ASR output to select a plausible form. Full fine-tuning reduces test word error rate (WER) from 48.6% to 17.1%; a 12-epoch run reaches 16.3%, compared with 16.4% for fine-tuned Whisper large-v3-turbo. Freezing the encoder increases WER to 25.5%, while excluding numeric clips raises WER on numeric test speech from 14.3% to 21.3%. We also evaluate on FLEURS using both its original references and mixed-script alternatives. The comparison shows that transcription conventions explain part, but not all, of the out-of-domain performance loss.
papers.venue: 9 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables. Code and model checkpoints: https://github.com/AI-Lab-Pvt-Ltd/nepali-codemixed-asr
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech foundation model

papers.title: Exploring Post-Hoc Disentanglement of Audio Foundation Models for Music Similarity
papers.abstract: Audio foundation models like CLAP, MuQ, and MERT excel at capturing general musical similarity. On the other hand, their entangled latent spaces limit interpretability and fine-grained attribute control. Conditional Similarity Networks (CSN) address this by pairing a backbone representation model with learned masks that gate the embedding space into attribute-specific subspaces. However, existing methods train the backbone from scratch, rather than leveraging pretrained foundation models. We instead present a systematic study of post-hoc disentanglement, adapting CSN to gate frozen pretrained embeddings. We evaluate adding trainable parameters to adapt the embedding under different masking and pooling regimes across two datasets. Our findings show that minimal adaptation capacity is sufficient for post-hoc gating to improve both attribute-specific disentanglement and overall retrieval performance, while pooling, masking, and depth choices yield limited additional gains.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio foundation model

papers.title: Which Acoustic Features Survive Compression? Tracker-Estimated First-Formant Statistics for Codec-Robust Audio DeepfakeDetection
papers.abstract: Audio deepfake detectors that work well on clean lab recordings often degrade after telephone or platform compression. This paper asks a specific question: which low-dimensional acoustic descriptors stay informative after codec degradation? We screen 36 utterance-level features(formants, PNCCs, LFCCs, prosody) on ASVspoof 2019 data and test on the official ASVspoof 2021 LA set across seven codec conditions. Of 33 statistically significant descriptors, only four show large practical separation (|r| >0.5, bootstrap 95% CIs), all first-formant (F1) measures, highly redundant (PC1: 79% variance). The payoff is stability: the 36-feature SVM degrades 14 pp under codec mismatch (9.5%-23.5% EER), while the four-feature RBF-SVM degrades only 5.9 pp (17.0%-22.9%). The F1 subset varies 3.4 pp across conditions versus 13.1 pp for the full set. F1 differences persist after controlling for speaker identity (p greater than 10^10, mixed-effects model). The results suggest that physically interpretable F1 statistics offer a compact, codec-stable diagnostic signal that may complement higher accuracy neural detectors.
reasons: Evaluation, Alignment, Safety & Copyright: audio deepfake

papers.title: Emilia2: A Large-Scale Dataset for Controllable Long-Form Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Generating long-form speech requires models to keep content, speaker identity, turn-taking, and expressive style consistent over time. Yet most open training corpora contain examples lasting only tens of seconds and open long-form benchmarks cover at most two speakers per recording. We introduce Emilia2, a 229K-hour multilingual dataset for controllable long-form speech generation. From in-the-wild data, Emilia2 constructs short utterances, single-speaker long-form speech, and multi-speaker dialogues, preserving transcripts, speaker identities, pauses, and acoustic transitions. Examples longer than five minutes account for 50.0% of single-speaker long-form hours and 66.8% of dialogue hours. To support expressive control, Emilia2 provides natural language instructions for 4.77M examples and nonverbal-vocalization tags for 933K examples. We also introduce Emilia2-testset, 23 hours of bilingual recordings of up to 30 minutes and four speakers, each speaker paired with reference audio. We train autoregressive (AR) and non-autoregressive (NAR) models on Emilia2. Our 0.6B-backbone NAR model achieves the lowest Chinese CER and English WER on TTSD-Eval (5.27%/9.93%) among compared systems, while our AR model is on par with Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-VD on InstructTTSEval (zh/en: 76.2/78.3 vs. 77.1/77.9). These results validate Emilia2 as a comprehensive data foundation for long-form speech generation and minute-scale expressive control. Demo: https://charlesnii.github.io/Emilia2-demo/.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech generation

papers.title: DialInstruct-TTS: Interactive Expressive Speech Generation via Multi-Turn Dialogue with Fine-Grained Temporal Control
papers.abstract: Existing instruction-based TTS systems primarily support one-shot, utterance-level control, where a single instruction determines the speaking style of an entire utterance. As a result, even minor refinements require rewriting the instruction and regenerating the full utterance, limiting fine-grained interactive control. We propose DialInstruct-TTS, an interactive multi-turn expressive TTS framework that enables users to iteratively refine generated speech through natural-language dialogue until the desired style is achieved. At each dialogue turn, a Qwen-based planner integrates the dialogue history and latest user instruction into a complete TemporalPlan, while a temporal acoustic control module provides fine-grained control over emotion, speaking rate, volume, and phonation. Reference-latent revision preserves non-target regions across turns, allowing users to modify only the requested attributes or temporal spans while retaining previously satisfactory speech. Subjective evaluations demonstrate improved global instruction following, accurate local style realization, and effective non-target preservation. Compared with conventional one-shot interaction requiring full instruction restatement and utterance regeneration, DialInstruct-TTS substantially improves perceived convenience and interaction comfort. Audio samples are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/eacl-demo-17C5/.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech generation

papers.title: Antalia-2 Mini: A 7.6-million-parameter Turkish text-to-speech model trained entirely on synthetic speech
papers.abstract: Antalia-2 Mini is a single-voice Turkish text-to-speech model with 7,620,931 parameters. It reads characters and produces 48 kHz audio at 41 times real time on an Apple M5 laptop CPU (2 threads). Its training audio came only from VoxCPM2 (the teacher), about 300 times larger, cloning one synthetic clip; automatic checks kept about 1,790 h. Fine-tuning the vocoder on the acoustic model's own mel spectrograms cut the word error rate (WER) of Whisper's transcripts from a mean of 3.89% to 1.75% at adjacent pre-release checkpoints. The teacher corrupts the start of a clip when the first word begins with \"o, the student learned this, and a spoken prefix we cut from the output hides it. On the 495-sentence Freya-TR-Eval benchmark, where we tuned settings, version 1.0.1 has WER 1.09% and character error rate 0.22% on our public harness. A paired bootstrap cannot distinguish these from EMA Lightning, an 8.6M Turkish model, which scores higher on full-band UTMOS, an English-trained quality proxy. No human listening test exists. Weights, inference code and the benchmark harness are public under Apache-2.0; training code and data are not.
papers.venue: 38 pages, 22 figures, 9 tables. Weights, inference code and benchmark harness: https://huggingface.co/cloud0day3/antalia-mini

AURA: Auditory Spatial Intelligence via a Unified Representation from a General-Audio Encoder through Complete Alignment
papers.abstract: Answering spatial questions about multi-source scenes requires a model both to identify each sound and to locate it. Existing spatial audio-language models obtain spatial information from a dedicated encoder, which separates spatial and semantic processing into distinct feature spaces. We study whether a general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can serve both purposes. A controlled layer-wise analysis shows that the frozen codec retains spatial information, with lateral cues carried by the difference between the two ear channels. This information, however, is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and, on the remaining axes, assigns the detected direction to the queried and the non-queried source equally often. We attribute this failure to an audio--text information asymmetry, in which the audio contains both sources while the answer describes only the queried one. A controlled $2\times2$ experiment shows that either completing the scene description or exposing the inter-channel difference lifts left/right accuracy above chance, whereas binding directions to the queried source requires both. Building on these findings, AURA keeps the codec and the language model frozen and exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy, with about 40\% of its trainable parameters.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio-language model

papers.title: Omni-JEV: Text and Dual-Stream Speech Decisions
papers.abstract: A user utterance does not uniquely determine the next action in full-duplex dialogue: its consequences depend on the assistant's response state and interaction history. Speech activity, utterance completion, and interruption intent provide related evidence, whose implications for a response require an explicit action policy. We formulate this task at collected-segment endpoints and introduce Omni-JEV, which maps text or role-indexed user and assistant-reference speech to probabilities over five interaction actions. An aligned speech-to-speech understanding backbone encodes the acoustic roles separately and shares its candidate readout with text inputs. Bilingual weak supervision supports cross-entropy fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning for probability-sensitive decisions (RLCD). We compare Gaussian-logit and categorical Choice RLCD from the same supervised initialization under matched training exposure, observing different trade-offs between classification and probability quality. Gaussian Omni-JEV achieves test accuracies of 84.08% for audio and 96.55% for text. This common action interface supports decisions about when a full-duplex voice assistant should respond, preserve ongoing speech, interrupt, or resume an interrupted response.

papers.title: Dyship: Leveraging Acoustic Features For Speaker Relationship Classification From Dyadic Conversations
papers.abstract: We introduce DyShip, a framework for classifying speaker familiarity and kinship from dyadic conversations in the Seamless Interaction corpus. We compare five speech representations: spectrograms, MFCCs, self-supervised WavLM representations, x-vectors, and estimated articulatory movements. Spectral features perform best for familiarity classification, reaching an accuracy of 87.81%, while WavLM achieves the highest kinship accuracy of 85.17%. X-vectors and articulatory features yield weaker results on familiarity classifiaction, but shine for kinship classification, with an AUC of 0.909 for x-vectors. Most classifiers exceed previously reported human and audio language model scores on the same dataset. These findings highlight the potential of conventional acoustic features for relationship inference and motivate further investigation of the conversational cues captured by different representations.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio language model

papers.title: Swanada: Split-Encoder Capability-Routed Conformer CTC and Sub-30 MB On-Device Speech Recognition Across Twelve Scripts
papers.abstract: Client-side automatic speech recognition (ASR) across Indic and Classical scripts eliminates cloud transcription costs, network tail latency, and server-side audio retention, yet neural exports face four systems bottlenecks in browsers and mobile runtimes: (1) monolithic per-language Conformer checkpoints require ~177 MiB per script (> 2.1 GiB across 12 scripts), exhausting CacheStorage quotas; (2) static relative positional encoding tables embed 10.2-20.5 MB of FP32 constants while 1x1 Conv1d layers trigger slow or unsupported ConvInteger kernels in WebAssembly SIMD; (3) sliding-window CTC flickers on boundary tokens; and (4) mobile WebAudio pipelines suffer 44.1/48 kHz sample-rate mismatches and silent AudioWorklet stalls under iOS WKWebView. We present Swanada, an open-source 16 kHz streaming ASR system spanning Classical Sanskrit, Indian English, and ten Indian languages (sa, en, hi, kn, mr, bn, ta, te, ml, gu, pa, or) across browser WebAssembly, Node.js, and Python. Swanada pairs capability-routed shared INT8 Conformer encoders (a 17-layer 177.38 MiB Studio tier at $d = 512$ for desktop/servers and a distilled 14-layer 25.35 MiB Mobile tier at $d = 256$ for phones) with twelve hot-swappable 515.0 KiB native-script linear CTC heads ($257 \times 512$), cutting 12-language storage by $11.6\times$ (183.4 MiB) and $67.8\times$ (31.39 MiB; 25.85 MiB first load). Runtime protobuf tail surgery exposes the shared representation in $< 2$ ms, while dynamic positional synthesis, MatMul pointwise convolutions, and post-quantization QInt8 head calibration preserve sub-30 MB accuracy. Across $N = 480$ held-out and $N = 1,280$ open public test clips (FLEURS, LibriSpeech, GLOBE, AMI, wild Sanskrit), Swanada achieves 5.43% held-out and 8.87% 12-language open CER on Studio (18.56% and 19.23% on Mobile) at $0.0097\times$-$0.0264\times$ RTF, with 30.6 ms median TTFT and 0.00% committed-prefix churn.
papers.venue: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Open-source browser, NodeJS, and Python implementation with interactive demo at https://hemanth.github.io/swanada/ and https://github.com/hemanth/swanada
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: automatic speech recognition

papers.title: FaiSonic MMD: A popular music dataset with temporally aligned multidimensional annotations for multitask music analysis
papers.abstract: Temporal analysis in music information retrieval concerns the positions of musical events and structures within recordings. Joint modeling has demonstrated the value of combining musical descriptions, but existing resources differ in joint coverage and expert verification across dimensions, constraining detailed joint supervision and the analysis of relationships on the same recordings. To support multitask modeling and the study of relationships among musical dimensions in popular music, we introduce FaiSonic Multidimensional Music Dataset (FaiSonic MMD), containing 500 songs totaling approximately 32.86 hours, comprising 250 Chinese-language and 250 English-language songs. Professional musicians annotate phrases, sections, chords, and rhythm in real recordings, followed by independent review. Events and intervals across dimensions share a recording-based time reference while retaining their respective musical granularity and boundaries, allowing direct comparison across musical descriptions. We describe the annotations, collection procedure, and statistics, and establish a comprehensive multitask baseline for phrase boundaries, section boundaries, section functions, chords, beats, and downbeats. We report reference performance for all prediction targets. FaiSonic MMD provides shared expert annotations and accompanying benchmarks for temporal music analysis.
papers.venue: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Dataset and code available at https://github.com/Kreuzter0421/FaiSonic-MMD
reasons: Music Foundation Models & Representations: music information retrieval

papers.title: ESDCodec: Ultra-Low Bitrate Speech Codec with Enhanced Semantic Disentanglement and Subband Decoding
papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in neural speech codecs, achieving highfidelity speech reconstruction at low bitrates remains a formidable challenge. To address this limitation, we propose ESDCodec, a speech codec that integrates a thoroughly enhanced semantic quantizer and a conditioned decoder network. Specifically, we employ a randomly initialized and frozen codebook, followed by a lightweight projector, to encode semantic details entirely within a linear space while enhancing codebook utilization. To further improve perceptual quality, we design a condition network that explicitly injects prior subband knowledge into the upsampling decoder. Taking the de-quantized feature as input, this network predicts subband signals, thereby providing fine-grained guidance for waveform reconstruction. Extensive experimental results show that ESDCodec achieves superior reconstruction performance at an ultra-low bitrate of 0.85kbps. For LLM-based speech generation tasks, ESDCodec also consistently outperforms existing codec models.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech generation

**An LLM Is All You Need: Data-Efficient Adaptation to Full-Duplex, Word-Level Spoken Dialogue** [![Project Page](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blog-Project%20Page-orange)](https://avera-labs.github.io/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni/) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Code-blue)](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni) [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97-Model-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/openmartdev/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni) [![Base model](https://img.shields.io/badge/Base-Qwen3--Omni--30B--A3B--Instruct-green)](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct) Tairan Chen, Richard Yucheng He, Yihang Liu, Baodong Cao, Chen Xu · [AveraLabs](https://averalabs.com/)
## Model Description Full-duplex voice models can listen and speak at the same time, so they can backchannel, yield the floor when they are interrupted, and take it back, the way people do. This behavior is usually learned by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. That training is costly and rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and turn-taking still ends up implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. **Awaken is based on [Qwen3-Omni](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct)**, keeping the multimodal LLM frozen and adapting it with little data into the thinker of a word-level full-duplex thinker–talker system on an 80 ms frame clock, while a separate talker turns the thinker's tokens into speech.

### Key Features - **Data-efficient**: Keeps [Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct) frozen and trains only 97.4M parameters: attention LoRA (13.4M), a user-audio adapter (75.5M), a channel-fusion layer (8.4M) and 17 timing-token embeddings. A four-stage curriculum performs the conversion in about 30 GPU-hours (30.5 on one NVIDIA B200), and no training run uses more than a few tens of thousands of dialogues. The adaptation needs no large-scale speech training (Qwen3-Omni itself was pretrained on large amounts of audio). - **Word-level turn-taking**: Every 80 ms the thinker emits one token of agent text. Pauses, yields (`SS`) and onsets (`SE`) are tokens of the same vocabulary, and a finite-state machine masks illegal tokens before sampling. The model decides every turn itself, with no external voice-activity detector. - **Competitive with large-scale speech training**: Among open-source full-duplex systems, it is the least likely to take the floor when the user merely pauses (turn-over rate **0.170**, against 0.584 for the next best) and it backchannels most often (**0.073** per second) on Full-Duplex-Bench v1.0. Among them, it also has the lowest response latency in every overlap scenario of Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5. On InteractionBench it leads them on groundedness (**53%**, against 35% for the next best), coherence (**47**) and spoken tasks (**26%**).

### Training Recipe

The LLM's weights, token embeddings and language-modeling head stay frozen throughout. Each stage trains a few added parameters and starts from the one before it; from Stage 3 on, a KL term at word positions holds what the model says close to the model the stage started from. 1. **Stage 1, audio alignment**: trains only the audio adapter, first as a speech-recognition read-out on 17,210 windows of user speech, then by distillation against the frozen LLM listening through its own audio encoder. 2. **Stage 2, pause timing**: adds `PAD`, `EPAD` and 13 pause tokens with rank-16 LoRA, on 760 single-turn spoken questions whose answers carry word-level pauses. 3. **Stage 3, turn-taking**: adds `SS` and `SE` and moves to the two-channel format, by self-distillation and then a multi-turn retrain on 12,146 dialogues that also trains the channel-fusion layer and the audio adapter. 4. **Stage 4, barge-in and backchannel**: trains on 36,621 dialogues with injected user interruptions, then on 42,229 sequences: those dialogues plus 701 backchannel dialogues repeated eight times. The **talker** is trained separately, in one supervised stage of 2.65 hours on one NVIDIA B200, on 36,996 examples of synthesized dialogue speech. Their word-level transcripts use the thinker's token format, so no thinker is needed to make the data. See the paper for the data and training details; the [project page](https://avera-labs.github.io/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni/) has an overview. ## Model Details | Attribute | Value | |-----------|-------| | Model Size | Thinker: frozen Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B thinker + 97.4M trained parameters; talker: 8-layer temporal (width 4,096) + 6-layer depth transformer (width 1,024) | | Base Model | [Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct) (turn-based, kept frozen); talker lineage from [PersonaPlex](https://github.com/NVIDIA/personaplex) | | Backbone | Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B mixture-of-experts thinker, one position per 80 ms frame (12.5 Hz) | | Input | Streaming 24 kHz user audio, encoded by the frozen [Mimi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16) codec (8 codebooks per frame) and read through a trained audio adapter | | Output | One agent-text token per frame; a Moshi-style talker voices it 3 frames (240 ms) later as 8 Mimi codebooks, decoded to 24 kHz speech | | Interaction | Full-duplex: backchannels, yields to barge-in and takes the floor back; no voice-activity detector | | Languages | English | | License | Code: Apache 2.0. The profile md5-pins every file under `checkpoints/` and `data/` except `data/thinker_text_emb.pt`, and the engine refuses to start on a mismatch. Not included, because they download from their own repositories on first use: [`Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct) (about 70 GB) and the Mimi codec in [`kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16`](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16). ## Requirements - Linux with one NVIDIA GPU and a driver that supports CUDA 12.8 - Measured on one H200 (141 GB): the demo peaked at about 112 GB, more than an 80 GB card holds (the thinker's bf16 weights alone take about 60 GB), and ran at a real-time factor of about 0.66 (p90 per-frame compute 52.6 ms per 80 ms frame) - Python 3.10 - PyTorch 2.8 with CUDA 12.8 (uv installs the cu128 wheels) - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) ## Installation ```bash git clone https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni cd AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni uv sync # .venv with Python 3.10; torch cu128 wheels come from the PyTorch index source .venv/bin/activate # puts awaken-server, awaken-offline, awaken-client and hf on PATH ``` uv is required: `moshi==0.2.13` declares `huggingface-hub<1.0` while transformers 5.x needs 1.x, and `pyproject.toml` overrides that bound for uv, which pip cannot do. ## Quick Start ### Download Models ```bash hf download openmartdev/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni --local-dir ./pretrained_models/awaken-omni ``` `hf` comes with `huggingface-hub`, a dependency of this package, so it is on PATH in the activated venv. The download is about 7.9 GB: the thinker, the talker, the default voice prompt and two tables. [Files](#files) lists them. `pretrained_models/` is git-ignored in the code repository. The base models are fetched from Hugging Face automatically on first use: [`Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct) (about 70 GB) and the Mimi codec from [`kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16`](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16). ### Inference Live server with the browser client built in (one conversation at a time, WebSocket protocol in `src/duplexaudio/serving/realtime/protocol.py` of the [code repository](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni)): ```bash awaken-server --model ./pretrained_models/awaken-omni --port 8998 # remote GPU box: ssh -L 8998:localhost:8998 , then open http://localhost:8998 in Chrome or Edge ``` `--model` also takes the Hugging Face repo id (`--model openmartdev/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni`), which fetches only `checkpoints/` and `data/` into the Hugging Face cache. The first start checks the md5 pins, loads the weights, compiles and warms up, which takes a few minutes. The server binds loopback only by default. There is no authentication, and every conversation is recorded under `logs/demo/sessions/` (in `$DUPLEX_RUNTIME_ROOT`, else the repository root, never in the model folder; `--rec-root DIR` changes it). Use headphones, or keep the page's default noise suppression and echo cancellation. Headless client, which streams a wav file through a running server (`--url`, default `ws://127.0.0.1:8998/ws`) at real-time pace: ```bash awaken-client --wav in.wav --out client_out/ # client_out/stereo.wav (L user, R agent), agent.wav, client.json ``` Offline, with a recorded user track (one process, no server): ```bash awaken-offline --model ./pretrained_models/awaken-omni --input user.wav --out offline_out/ # stereo.wav, transcript.txt, recordings ``` `--out` must be a new or empty folder. `stereo.wav` has the user on the left and the agent on the right, and `transcript.txt` holds the agent's text, one line per turn. From Python: ```python from duplexaudio import RealtimeEngine, load_profile, set_model_dir set_model_dir("./pretrained_models/awaken-omni") # or the HF repo id; call before load_profile / RealtimeEngine eng = RealtimeEngine(load_profile("default")) eng.run(eng.load) # md5 pins, weights, compile + warm-up (a few minutes) sess = eng.run(eng.new_session, "demo") # clean context + per-conversation seeds for frame in frames: # float32 (1920,): 80 ms of 24 kHz mono user audio out = eng.run(sess.tick, frame) # out.pcm: int16 agent audio of out.agent_frame; out.text, out.kind eng.run(sess.flush) # voice the talker's last words after the input ends meta = eng.run(sess.finalize, "stop") # grammar + talker-input checks, timings, recordings ``` ## Evaluation We run the full system end to end on two external benchmarks of real-time behavior. The per-seed values are in the paper's appendix, and the [project page](https://avera-labs.github.io/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni/) has an overview. ## Inference Details
How the inference stack works Every 80 ms ("one frame", 12.5 Hz) the engine * encodes the newest 80 ms of user audio with Mimi's streaming encoder into 8 codebook indices. The thinker's **audio adapter** embeds them, and the **channel-fusion** layer combines them with the agent's previous token; * runs one step of the frozen **Qwen3-Omni thinker** (with LoRA) and samples one agent token under the **turn-taking state machine**'s mask. The token is a word piece, a pause token, `PAD` (nothing new this frame), `SS` (silence start: the agent yields) or `SE` (silence end: the agent takes the floor). While the agent is silent the only legal choice is `PAD` or `SE`; within its turn, the choice is a word, a pause or `SS`; * passes the token id to the **talker**, which reads the text 3 frames (240 ms) ahead of the audio it produces. A canonicalizer table (`data/talker_canon.json`) maps thinker tokens the talker never saw in training onto ones it did, and pause tokens reach it as `PAD`. One step of its temporal transformer and depth transformer emits the 8 Mimi codebooks of the next agent frame; * decodes those codes with Mimi's streaming decoder into agent speech. ``` mic 24 kHz ─► Mimi encoder ─► 8 user codes / frame ─► audio adapter ─┐ ▼ previous agent token ─────────────────────────────► channel fusion ▲ │ │ ▼ │ Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B thinker (frozen) + LoRA │ │ state-machine mask │ ▼ └──────────────────────── next agent token: word / pause / PAD / SS / SE │ token ids only ▼ talker: temporal + depth transformer, text 3 frames ahead │ 8 agent codes / frame ▼ Mimi decoder ─► speaker ``` Both halves run a step every frame, including during silence, which is what lets the agent be interrupted and backchannel. The user channel is never muted or gated. Every CUDA call of a conversation runs on one GPU thread (`src/duplexaudio/serving/realtime/engine.py`), and the thinker's single-frame step is CUDA-graphed (`src/duplexaudio/inference/thinker/fast_thinker.py`).
Decode parameters One profile, `src/duplexaudio/serving/realtime/profiles/default.yaml`, fixes the released files and every decode setting. The loader rejects missing and unknown keys, so no value can drift in silently from code. | Part | Setting | Value | |------|---------|-------| | Thinker | temperature while silent (whether to take the floor) | 0.0 (greedy) | | | temperature while speaking | 0.2 | | | repetition control | penalty 1.2 on the last 24 tokens, no repeated 3-gram | | | `SS` / `SE` logit bias | 0.0 / 0.0 | | | KV cache | 4,096 positions | | Talker | text lead | 3 frames (240 ms) | | | sampler | temperature 0.8, top-k 250 | | | voice prompt | `data/default_vp_codes.npy` with its frame-aligned transcript `data/default_vp_text.npy` | | Front end | room-tone floor under the user channel | −78 to −63 dBFS, as in the Stage-4 training data | | Session | length cap | 3,000 frames (240 s), lowered to what the caches can hold | To change a setting, or to use your own voice prompt, copy the profile, edit it (paths and md5s) and pass `--profile path/to/profile.yaml`. Profile paths are not relative to the working directory: `data/...` and `checkpoints/...` resolve inside the `--model` folder, so give your own files as absolute paths.
Model folder and file pins `--model DIR` (or `set_model_dir`) serves the model files from a folder laid out like the Hugging Face repo: ``` checkpoints/thinker/model.pt thinker: audio adapter, channel fusion, LoRA and timing-token weights checkpoints/thinker/persona.txt thinker system prompt checkpoints/talker/model.safetensors talker data/thinker_text_emb.pt the thinker's token-embedding table, read by the talker at load data/default_vp_codes.npy, data/default_vp_text.npy default voice prompt: Mimi codes + frame-aligned transcript data/talker_canon.json talker input canonicalizer table ``` Every file above except `data/thinker_text_emb.pt` is md5-pinned in the profile, as is `configs/talker.yaml` in the code repository, and the engine refuses to start on a mismatch. Without `--model`, the files are read from `checkpoints/` and `data/` under `$DUPLEX_RUNTIME_ROOT`, else under the code repository's root; if neither folder is there, `awaken-server` and `awaken-offline` stop at once and ask for `--model`.
Repository layout In the [code repository](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni): ``` src/duplexaudio/ __init__.py the Python API: RealtimeEngine, load_profile, set_model_dir common/paths.py repository, runtime and model-folder paths (set_model_dir) models/thinker/ timing tokens, text format, user-audio front end, LoRA, dense mixture-of-experts forward models/talker/ the talker: a Moshi LMModel whose text input is the thinker's token stream inference/thinker/ frame-by-frame KV-cached engine, CUDA-graphed step, turn-taking state machine, loader inference/talker/ talker loader, inputs, voice prompt, canonicalizer table, sampler serving/realtime/ profile, engine, session loop, streaming Mimi, thinker and talker steps, server.py (awaken-server, browser client in static/), offline.py (awaken-offline), client.py (awaken-client) profiles/default.yaml the released profile: file pins and every decode setting configs/talker.yaml talker architecture (md5-pinned by the profile) tests/ CPU tests, no GPU or checkpoints needed hf_model_card/ Hugging Face model card (README + figures) index.html project page ``` Run the tests with `uv sync --extra dev && pytest`.
## Limitations - **English only.** - **Synthetic voices.** The talker was trained on synthesized speech and speaks in a synthetic voice. - **Background noise.** Turn-taking was evaluated on benchmark audio and can degrade under loud background noise. - **Content quality.** Responses after an interruption are rated less relevant than those of some baselines. - **Voice control.** The talker does not control loudness or whispering, and it speaks from the agent text alone: it does not yet condition its voice on how the user sounds. - **Safety.** No safety tuning beyond the base model's; not evaluated for harmful-content behavior. ## Intended use and out-of-scope use - **Intended:** research on full-duplex spoken dialogue. - **Out of scope:** - impersonating real people or cloning someone's voice without consent; - presenting the agent as a human; - high-stakes use (medical, legal or financial advice), or use where a wrong turn-taking decision could cause harm. ## License The code is licensed under the [Apache 2.0 License](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni/blob/main/LICENSE). The model weights in this repository are distributed separately from the code, and their license has not been decided yet. The base models downloaded at run time keep their own licenses; see [`NOTICE`](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni/blob/main/NOTICE). ## Acknowledgments The thinker is built on the frozen thinker of [Qwen3-Omni](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct) (Apache 2.0). See [`NOTICE`](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni/blob/main/NOTICE). ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{chen2026llm, title = {An {LLM} Is All You Need: Data-Efficient Adaptation to Full-Duplex, Word-Level Spoken Dialogue}, author = {Tairan Chen and Richard Yucheng He and Yihang Liu and Baodong Cao and Chen Xu}, year = {2026}, howpublished = {\url{https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni}} } ``` ## Contact - 🐛 Submit an [Issue](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni/issues) - 💡 Submit a [Pull Request](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex-Qwen3Omni/pulls)

--- license: other license_name: mixed-non-commercial license_link: LICENSE.md tags: - music-generation - yue2 - gguf - text-to-image - ruach-studio - text-to-music - song-generation - lyrics-to-song - suno-alternative library_name: ggml base_model: m-a-p/YuE2-3B base_model_relation: quantized pipeline_tag: text-to-audio --- # Ruach Studio · Models v2

Website · GitHub · The guide · ☕ Buy me a Coffee Machine

> Ruach Studio is open music generation that runs on your own hardware: the model, the score, the adapters and every take stay yours, and nothing is rented by the token. Open models are now good enough to stand on their own, and what was missing is the studio around them: that is what we build, in the open. Music should be free to make and to share: whoever has no voice, no instrument and no studio still has the right to lay their thoughts and feelings onto sound. > **⚠ Not on free cloud GPUs.** Ruach Studio does not run on Google Colab, Kaggle or any free notebook GPU, so don't spend an evening on it there: it is a whole studio, not a notebook. It builds its C++/CUDA engine on the machine it lives on, keeps a server and a lab of Python services running beside it, and takes about 33 GB of disk (60 GB with the Artist). A free session's card, memory, wiped disk and hours-long limit cannot hold that. It wants your own Linux computer, or a server you rent and keep, with an NVIDIA card: 24 GB for everything, 16 GB with the smaller model copies. Everything [Ruach Studio](https://github.com/igrbible/Ruach_Studio) runs on, in one place and laid out as its own folders: the music model and its decoders, the transcriber, the stems' and the sound upscaler's models, Whisper, the style listener, the studio's own adapters, the LoRA Trainer's base, and the Artist's painters with the adapters their authors let be shared. 1662 files, 501 GB. A copy of the studio's own disk, file for file: what lies here is what it paints, sings and trains with, and the studio fetches all of it from here alone. **Nothing here is ours but the conversions and the studio's own adapters.** Every other file is its authors' work, unchanged, under its authors' licence, credited below and line by line in `MANIFEST.tsv`. Not affiliated with M-A-P, Comfy Org, Mothersuperior, HaileyStorm, atomtanstudio, storagejuju, OpenAI, Systran, Meta, the Qwen team, Unsloth, lightx2v, Falconsai, prithivMLmods, Civitai or the authors named below. If you are an author and want a file of yours taken down, open a discussion here and it goes. ## Take what you need The studio's own install (`./fetch-models.sh`) takes what your card can run, at a pinned revision, checking each file. # StaleyNET checkpoints

[![Source on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/source-GitHub-1D1B20?logo=github)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet) [![staleynet-audio on crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/staleynet-audio?label=staleynet-audio)](https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/paper-PDF-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/blob/main/paper/preprint.pdf) [![Book](https://img.shields.io/badge/book-mdBook-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/tree/main/book/src) [![Release v0.1.2](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/arpanpathak/staleynet)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases) [![Dataset: 3.1 GB](https://img.shields.io/badge/dataset-3.1%20GB-FFD21E?logo=huggingface&logoColor=black)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/arpanpathak/staleynet-data)

Weights for **StaleyNET**, a text-prompted music generator trained from random initialization in Rust on NVIDIA edge GPUs. The Transformer, residual vector quantizer, Griffin-Lim vocoder, and GPU kernels are implemented in the project.

The code, paper, and book live in the companion repository:
<https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet>.

## Release v0.1.2

- GitHub release: <https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases/tag/v0.1.2>
- `staleynet-audio` 0.1.2 on crates.io: <https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio>. Its page explains each audio step with intuition and runnable examples.
- Since v0.1.1: the GPU kernels are organised into one module per topic, the AGX Thor builds against cuda-oxide's main branch, and the paper has been revised with hardware, benchmark and tokenizer appendices.
- New in these repositories: the `lyrics-thor`, `lyrics-thor-long` and `pq-large` runs, and the band-group token caches they train on.
- CI: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, cargo-deny, the audio coverage gate, and documentation tests for every example on the crate page.

## At a glance

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Checkpointed runs | 9 |
| Parameters | 7,099,904 for text-only runs; 7,165,440 for the lyrics runs; 42,858,496 for `pq-large` |
| Transformer | width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, context 768 (`pq-large`: width 512, 8 layers, context 1152) |
| Audio tokens | 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries (`pq-large`: 4 band groups × 4 levels = 16 codebooks of 1024 entries) |
| Audio features | 128 mel bands at 24 kHz, FFT 1024, hop 256 |
| Training data | Song Describer Dataset and JamendoLyrics MultiLang |
| License | CC BY-SA 4.0, subject to the upstream dataset terms |

## Checkpoints

| Run | Purpose | Parameters | `best` step | `latest` step | Training tracks |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `thor-base` | base text-to-music model | 7,099,904 | 0 | None | 667 |
| `smoke` | pipeline smoke test | 7,099,904 | 0 | 1,500 | 667 |
| `overfit-one-take` | single-take memorisation check | 7,099,904 | 200 | 200 | 1 |
| `vocal-scratch` | vocal-filtered model from scratch | 7,099,904 | 5,500 | 6,000 | 281 |
| `vocal-finetune` | vocal fine-tune | 7,099,904 | 250 | None | 281 |
| `lyrics-orin` | lyrics-conditioned model | 7,165,440 | 3,750 | 4,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor` | lyrics-conditioned model trained on the AGX Thor | 7,165,440 | 4,750 | 8,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor-long` | the same model trained for 20,000 steps | 7,165,440 | 19,750 | 20,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `pq-large` | larger model on the band-group tokenizer (in progress) | 42,858,496 | 7,000 | 7,000 | 742 (75 with lyrics) |

The step values are exactly what each `model.json` records. `best/` is the weight-only checkpoint selected by validation. `latest/` is the resumable checkpoint with AdamW moments. Some early runs stored only `best/`, and `thor-base` and `smoke` record step 0 in their `best/model.json`. Where a `latest/` exists, prefer it for the late training state.

### About `pq-large`

`pq-large` is still training on the Jetson AGX Thor (128 GB). The files here are a snapshot at step 7,000 of 20,000, and they will be replaced as the run advances. Its validation loss (5.135 nats per token at step 7,000) is averaged over 16 codebooks of a different tokenizer, so it cannot be compared directly with the 4-codebook runs above.

The model reads codes from the band-group tokenizer, which splits the 128 mel bands into 4 groups and quantises each group with 4 residual levels. That tokenizer is stored as `checkpoints/pq-large/tokenizer.json`, and the matching caches are `cache-g4l4f1/`, `cache-pq-jamendolyrics/` and `cache-pq-recordings/` in the dataset repository. Pass `--cache data/cache-g4l4f1` when generating with this run.

`evaluations/<run>/` holds the paired lyrics test of each lyrics run: the per-track loss with aligned, removed and mismatched lyrics.

## Training progress

The runs on the Jetson AGX Thor publish their metrics here every two hours
(`deploy/hf/publish.sh` in the code repository): `metrics/<run>.jsonl` holds
every logged event, and `plots/<run>.png` shows, from left to right, the
training and validation loss in nats per code against optimizer step, the
latest validation loss of each codebook (coarse levels are far easier to
predict than fine ones), and the throughput in positions per second.

![pq-large training curves](plots/pq-large.png)

## Layout

```text
checkpoints/<run>/best/      weights only       model.json + tensors.bin
checkpoints/<run>/latest/    weights + AdamW    model.json + tensors.bin
configs/                     canonical training configurations
run-configs/                 per-run config.json where the run saved one
metrics/                     full metrics.jsonl for every run
logs/                        captured training logs and the tokenizer sweeps
evaluations/<run>/           paired lyrics evaluations
```

`tensors.bin` is little-endian `f32` in parameter-visitor order. `latest/` appends the AdamW first moments and then the second moments. `model.json` records the tensor manifest, the step, whether optimizer state is present, and the training configuration.

## Download and use

```bash
hf download arpanpathak/staleynet-checkpoints \
  --repo-type model --local-dir staleynet-checkpoints

# From the code repository, on a Jetson with the cuda-oxide toolchain:
cargo oxide build -- --release
staleynet sing \
  --cache data/cache \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/thor-base/best \
  --prompt "slow acoustic ballad, warm female voice" \
  --out song.wav
```

For the lyrics model:

```bash
staleynet sing \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/lyrics-orin/best \
  --prompt "grunge rock, raw male voice" \
  --lyrics-file song.txt \
  --out song.wav
```

Architecture: width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, feed-forward multiplier 4, context length 768, 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries, 128 mel bands at 24 kHz. `lyrics-orin` adds a 256-byte lyrics field.

## Training data and licensing

- **Song Describer Dataset** (SDD), Zenodo record [10072001](https://zenodo.org/records/10072001): 706 Jamendo recordings with human captions. Captions are CC BY-SA 4.0. The recordings carry the per-track Creative Commons licenses in `audio_licenses.txt`, including CC BY-NC-ND and CC BY-NC-SA.
- **JamendoLyrics MultiLang**, <https://github.com/f90/jamendolyrics>: code and metadata are MIT. Songs and lyrics carry the per-song CC licenses in `JamendoLyrics.csv`.

Because the training audio includes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks, these checkpoints are research artifacts, not a commercial product. Do not use them commercially where the upstream recording licenses forbid it, and do not use them to impersonate a singer without consent.

The checkpoint files are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0 (`LICENSE-CC-BY-SA-4.0.txt`) to the extent the upstream dataset licenses allow. See `NOTICE` for the full provenance statement and `SHA256SUMS` for integrity.

## Known limitations

- Griffin-Lim produces phasey audio compared with a learned vocoder.
- The models are small edge models, not production music systems.
- The lyric models were trained on a small lyrics subset, so lyric intelligibility is limited.
- The checkpoints are research artifacts and have no warranty.

## Citation

```bibtex
@misc{pathak2026staleynet,
  author = {Arpan Pathak},
  title  = {StaleyNET: Text-Conditioned Music Generation Trained from Scratch
            on Edge GPUs in Rust},
  year   = {2026},
  url    = {https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet}
}
```

Confucius4-TTS: a Multilingual and Cross-Lingual Zero-Shot TTS Engine

One voice. Any language.

                                  

> [!IMPORTANT] > This repository is an aggregate distribution prepared for vLLM-Omni. It > includes Confucius4-TTS and its W2V-BERT 2.0, CAMPPlus, and BigVGAN runtime > dependencies. No single license covers the entire directory. ## Bundled vLLM-Omni Distribution The dependency weights are co-located so the package can be published and downloaded as one model directory: ```text Confucius4-TTS/ ├── t2s_model.safetensors ├── s2a_model.pt ├── wav2vec2bert_stats.pt ├── tokenizer.* ├── pretrained/ │ ├── w2v-bert-2.0/ │ └── campplus/ └── bigvgan/ ``` | Component | Pinned upstream revision | License | | --- | --- | --- | | Confucius4-TTS | `36b10dd6ff5026e333123bda5f6366de27c8b7a1` | Apache-2.0 | | W2V-BERT 2.0 | `da985ba0987f70aaeb84a80f2851cfac8c697a7b` | MIT | | CAMPPlus | `e4b6ede7ce16997aff4ae69fbca1f0175e2afede` | Apache-2.0 | | BigVGAN | `633ff708ed5b74903e86ff1298cf4a98e921c513` | MIT, with Apache-2.0-derived source files | Release and compliance metadata: * [Aggregate license notice](./LICENSE) * [Component license texts](./LICENSES/) * [Third-party notices](./THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) * [Pinned provenance and artifact hashes](./MODEL_PROVENANCE.json) * [Full-file checksum manifest](./SHA256SUMS) Verify a downloaded copy with: ```bash sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS ``` When publishing, exclude generated directories such as `pretrained/campplus/.cache/`; they are local download caches and are not part of this release. ### Responsible Use Voice cloning can reproduce a person's identity and speaking characteristics. Use reference audio only with the speaker's consent or another valid legal basis. Clearly disclose synthetic audio where appropriate, protect reference audio and generated voice data, and do not use this package for impersonation, fraud, harassment, or other harmful activity. Confucius4-TTS is an advanced LLM-based text-to-speech (TTS) system designed for multilingual and cross-lingual speech synthesis. Built on a speech encoder + large language model (LLM) architecture, Confucius4-TTS enables high-quality speech generation while preserving speaker identity across languages. You can try our online demo at **[https://confucius4-tts.youdao.com/gradio](https://confucius4-tts.youdao.com/gradio)**. **✨ Key Features** - **14 Languages Supported**: Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Spanish, Indonesian, Italian, Thai, Portuguese, Russian, Malay and Vietnamese *(more coming soon)* - **Unconstrained Voice Cloning**: No reference transcript required - **Cross-Lingual Voice Transfer**: Unaccented speech synthesis across 14 languages - **Zero-Shot Voice Transfer**: Clone voices without additional training - **Seamless Emotion Transfer**: Clone the feeling, not just the voice - **Robust Generalization**: Stable performance in real-world multilingual scenarios With strong cross-lingual generalization, Confucius4-TTS allows users to seamlessly switch languages while keeping the same voice, delivering fluent, natural, and expressive speech. ## Contents - [Installation](#-installation) - [Inference](#-inference) - [Training](#-training) - [Performance](#-performance) - [Citation](#citation) ## 🛠 Installation ### Requirements - Python 3.10 - CUDA 12.6 ### Setup 1. Clone the repository: ```bash git clone https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-TTS.git cd Confucius4-TTS ``` 2. Create and activate a conda environment: ```bash conda create -n confuciustts python=3.10 -y conda activate confuciustts ``` 3. Install dependencies: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` ## 🚀 Inference Use the provided `example.py` script for zero-shot TTS synthesis: ```bash python example.py \ --prompt_wav path/to/reference.wav \ --text "Your text to synthesize" \ --lang en \ --out output.wav \ --config config/inference_config.yaml ``` You can also use the Python API directly: ```python import torch import torchaudio from confuciustts.cli.inference import ConfuciusTTS model = ConfuciusTTS( config_path="config/inference_config.yaml", device="cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu", ) audio = model.generate( text="Hello, welcome to Confucius4-TTS.", lang="en", prompt_wav="path/to/reference.wav", verbose=True, ) torchaudio.save("output.wav", audio.cpu(), model.sample_rate) ``` ## 🚀 Fine-Tuning Confucius4-TTS follows a "speech encoder + LLM" architecture. The training pipeline covers two modules: - **Text2Semantic (T2S)**: generates semantic token sequences from text and speaker conditioning. - **Semantic2Acoustic (S2A)**: a flow-matching model that converts semantic tokens into mel spectrograms. ### 1. Prepare Pretrained Models Download the two external models: ```bash # Wav2Vec2-BERT (speaker conditioning & semantic feature extraction) huggingface-cli download facebook/w2v-bert-2.0 \ --local-dir pretrained/w2v-bert-2.0 # Amphion MaskGCT (semantic codec implementation) git clone https://github.com/open-mmlab/Amphion.git external/Amphion ``` After downloading, your directory should look like: ``` checkpoints/ ├── t2s_model.safetensors # pretrained T2S weights ├── s2a_model.pt # pretrained S2A weights ├── wav2vec2bert_stats.pt # semantic feature normalization statistics ├── special_tokens_map.json # tokenizer files ├── tokenizer.json ├── tokenizer.model └── tokenizer_config.json pretrained/ ├── w2v-bert-2.0/ # Wav2Vec2-BERT model └── campplus/ └── campplus_cn_common.bin # CAMPPlus speaker encoder checkpoint external/ └── Amphion/ # MaskGCT semantic codec implementation ``` ### 2. Prepare Training Data Training data is provided as **TSV files** (tab-separated, no header) with the following 5 columns: | Column | Description | |---|---| | `lang` | Language code (e.g. `zh`, `en`, `ja`) | | `wav_path` | Path to the target audio | | `norm_text` | Normalized text | | `semantic_ids_path` | Pre-extracted semantic tokens (`.npy` file path) | | `ref_audio_paths` | Reference audio path(s), comma-separated for multiple | Configure the train/validation paths in `config/train_t2s.yaml`: ```yaml data: train_data_path: - data/train.tsv val_data_path: - data/val.tsv ``` ### 3. Launch T2S Training Set the pretrained T2S checkpoint path in `config/train_t2s.yaml`: ```yaml paths: t2s_checkpoint: checkpoints/t2s_model.safetensors ``` **Single-node training:** ```bash python -m confuciustts.cli.train_t2s -c config/train_t2s.yaml ``` ### 4. Launch S2A Training Set the checkpoint paths in `config/train_s2a.yaml`. `t2s_checkpoint` points to the frozen T2S backbone; `s2a_checkpoint` is optional and can be used to resume from a pretrained S2A model: ```yaml paths: t2s_checkpoint: checkpoints/t2s_model.safetensors s2a_checkpoint: checkpoints/s2a_model.pt # optional: resume from pretrained S2A ``` **Single-node training:** ```bash python -m confuciustts.cli.train_s2a -c config/train_s2a.yaml ``` During S2A training, the T2S model, speaker encoder (Wav2Vec2-BERT), and style encoder (CAMPPlus) are all frozen. Only the flow-matching S2A model is trained. ## 📊 Performance Confucius4-TTS achieves competitive results on multilingual and cross-lingual zero-shot TTS benchmarks, with strong intelligibility and speaker similarity across multiple languages. > Lower is better for WER/CER (↓), and higher is better for SIM (↑). ### CV3-eval Cross-lingual
CV3-eval Cross-lingual Results (click to expand) | Direction | Metric | Confucius4-TTS | CosyVoice2† | CosyVoice3-0.5B† | CosyVoice3-1.5B† | OmniVoice† | VoxCPM2 | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | en→zh | CER↓ | **6.16** | 13.50 | 8.48 | 8.01 | 6.53 | 6.29 | | ja→zh | CER↓ | 4.87 | 48.10 | 6.86 | 6.78 | 52.64 | **4.20** | | ko→zh | CER↓ | 1.28 | 7.70 | 5.24 | 3.30 | 1.71 | **1.20** | | zh→en | WER↓ | **3.19** | 17.10 | 6.83 | 5.39 | 3.72 | 3.84 | | ja→en | WER↓ | **3.44** | 11.20 | 5.86 | 5.94 | 5.25 | 4.10 | | ko→en | WER↓ | **3.42** | 13.10 | 18.30 | 13.70 | 3.91 | 5.69 | † Requires reference text.

--- license: apache-2.0 pipeline_tag: text-to-speech library_name: zonos3 language: - en - fr - es - de - it - pt - nl - pl - ru - sv - tr - uk - cs - da - fi - el - hu - "no" - ro - sk - bg - zh - ja - ko - ar - he - vi - id - th - tl - ms - ka - hi - bn - ta - te - mr - gu - kn - ml - pa - or - ur tags: - text-to-speech - tts - speech-synthesis - voice-cloning - multilingual - gguf - zonos - zonos3 - zyphra --- # ZONOS3-Mini

--- ZONOS3-Mini is Zyphra’s compact, open-source text-to-speech model, delivering natural reliable speech and high-fidelity voice cloning with just 100 million active parameters. It runs in real time on phones and laptops, including directly in the browser. Clone a voice from an audio sample, or design a character by shaping age, accent and vocal texture. Steer emotion, pace and delivery down to individual words for games, narration and voice assistants. Run ZONOS3-Mini locally with our browser and native runtimes, or access it through [Zyphra Cloud](https://cloud.zyphra.com/models/zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini). Model weights are released under Apache 2.0. **Model details, samples and evaluations are in the [blog post](https://www.zyphra.com/our-work/zonos3-mini).** **A hosted version is available at [Zyphra Cloud](https://cloud.zyphra.com/models/zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini).** ## Languages ZONOS3-Mini supports 43 languages. | Region | Languages | |---|---| | Western and Southern Europe | English, French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Greek | | Northern Europe | Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, Finnish | | Central and Eastern Europe | Polish, Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Russian, Ukrainian | | Middle East and Caucasus | Turkish, Arabic, Hebrew, Georgian | | East Asia | Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Korean | | Southeast Asia | Vietnamese, Indonesian, Malay, Thai, Tagalog | | South Asia | Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi, Odia, Urdu | ## Quick start ### In your browser ZONOS3-Mini runs entirely on your own GPU through WebGPU: no install and no server. The first visit downloads the model, and the browser keeps it cached for later visits. You need a browser with WebGPU support. - [Zonos Voice Studio](https://zyphra.com/zonos3-mini/localplayground#cast): the full studio. - [Lite](https://zyphra.com/zonos3-mini/localplayground/lite): quick voice cloning. Pick, upload or record a voice and speak with it. ### With SGLang [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) serves ZONOS3-Mini on NVIDIA GPUs behind the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` endpoint, with streaming and voice cloning from a reference clip (no transcript needed). Install SGLang-Omni by following its [installation guide](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/get_started/installation.md), then start a server: ```bash sgl-omni serve --model-path Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini --port 8000 ``` Once `curl http://localhost:8000/health` reports `"healthy"`, generate speech with the default voice from another terminal: ```bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/speech \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"input": "Hello from ZONOS3-Mini!"}' \ --output output.wav ``` Add `"references": [{"audio_path": ""}]` to clone a voice, or `"stream": true, "response_format": "pcm"` to stream 44.1 kHz audio as it is generated. The [ZONOS3 cookbook](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/cookbook/zonos3.md) covers voice cloning, streaming and the sampling options. ### Native runtimes The [ZONOS3-Mini GitHub repository](https://github.com/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini) holds Zyphra's own runtimes, which share one HTTP API and serve the Zonos Voice Studio: a CUDA server for NVIDIA GPUs, an MLX server for Apple Silicon, a C++/ggml server and CLI (CPU, CUDA, Metal or Vulkan), and the in-browser WebGPU build. They load the GGUF files in [`gguf/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/tree/main/gguf) and the WebGPU shards in [`web/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/tree/main/web); the 27 default voices, grouped by language, are in [`gguf/voices/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/blob/main/gguf/voices/README.md). ## Architecture (rough outline) Text is NeMo-normalized (English, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese; other languages pass through as written) and encoded with an 8,192-entry SuperBPE tokenizer. The language model autoregressively generates 15 Hz dual-codec frames (10 codebooks of 4,096 entries each: one semantic codebook distilled from the Wav2Vec2-BERT teacher plus nine acoustic codebooks), conditioned on the text, a speaker prompt and three bucketed acoustic controls. A causal multi-resolution iSTFT head renders the frames to 44.1 kHz audio as they are produced. ![ZONOS3-Mini inference pipeline](assets/zonos3_mini_arloop_animated.gif) *Inference pipeline. Speaker conditioning (raw reference codes or a speaker-embedding row), control rows and SuperBPE text enter the hybrid GDN/attention MoE backbone, which predicts all ten codebooks of the next frame under the delay pattern (four drawn); as soon as a frame's last codebook is generated, the codec's causal iSTFT head renders that frame to audio.* | | ZONOS3-Mini | |---|---| | Backbone | 11 layers, model dim 1,024; 800M parameters total, about 100M active per token (latent MoE: 64 experts, top-2 routing, from layer 1) | | Sequence mixer | pattern `gdn3_global1`: 9 Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers + 2 global attention layers (16 heads x 32 dims, 4 KV heads), attention residuals (`full_attnres`); context 32,768 positions | | Text | SuperBPE, 8,192 entries (+4 specials), NeMo text normalization at inference | | Audio tokens | 15 Hz, 44.1 kHz dual-encoding codec, 10 x 4,096 codebooks (1 semantic + 9 acoustic); hop 2,940 samples; up to 10 minutes of audio per generation | | Speaker prompt | raw reference clip (encoded by the codec into a token prefix, up to 60 s, with speaker CFG) **or** a single 192-d MECT-B2 speaker embedding (`ownmect_s2`) | | Controls | loudness (LUFS, 10 buckets), bandwidth f_max (Hz, 10 buckets), **speaking rate (UTF-8 bytes per second, 30 buckets)**; each row has an "unknown" index; bucket edges in `params.json` (`condition_edges`) | | Decoder | causal multi-resolution iSTFT head: `full_mr` (default) or `keep2_plain` (pruned, about 3x faster decode) | | Precision | bf16 weights (`model.pth`); decoder heads run in fp32 | ![ZAC 1 audio codec](assets/arch_zac1_dark.png) *ZAC 1 (Zyphra Audio Codec 1).* ## Evaluations Full results and the ZTTS2 capability index are in the [blog post](https://www.zyphra.com/our-work/zonos3-mini#evaluation). Quality against speed on one H100 80GB. Quality combines macro speaker similarity and macro WER over the 55 language subsets of [ZTTS2-Eval](https://zyphra.github.io/ZTTS2-Eval/) (benchmark version 2: FLEURS-R read speech in 35 languages and VoxBlink2 in-the-wild recordings in 20 languages) as ½ z(similarity) − ½ z(WER) across the systems shown; ZONOS3-Mini is measured with the speaker-embedding prompt. Left: median time to first audio with 8 concurrent requests (80 ms for ZONOS3-Mini). Right: peak throughput at each model's best concurrency (457 seconds of audio per second for ZONOS3-Mini). ![ZONOS3-Mini quality versus time to first audio and throughput](assets/eval_pareto.png) ## Citation If you find this model useful in an academic context, please cite the release post: ``` @misc{zyphra2026zonos3mini, title = {{ZONOS3-Mini Technical Report}}, author = {Gabriel Clark and Sofian Mejjoute and George Close and Beren Millidge}, year = {2026}, month = nov, howpublished = {\url{https://www.zyphra.com/our-work/zonos3-mini}}, } ```

# M5-TTS

English | [简体中文](README_zh.md)

[GitHub](https://github.com/ASLP-lab/M5-TTS) · [Demo](https://aslp-lab.github.io/M5-TTS-Demo-Page/) · [Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ASLP-lab/M5-TTS-Space) · [Models](https://huggingface.co/collections/ASLP-lab/m5-tts)

**M5-TTS** is a compact multilingual and multi-dialect text-to-speech system from ASLP@NPU and LycheeAI Lab. It combines a 30M temporal backbone with a 20M local multi-token prediction decoder, using 16 audio codebooks at 12.5 frames/s for **24 kHz** speech generation. The speech codec is separate.

**Supported languages and dialects:** Mandarin Chinese · English · German · French · Japanese · Korean · Cantonese · Sichuanese.

This repository provides the reference-based voice-cloning checkpoint. It supports Chinese, English, German, French, Japanese and Korean, with Cantonese and Sichuan dialect conditioning. For preset-speaker synthesis without reference audio, use [M5-TTS-50M-CustomVoice](https://huggingface.co/ASLP-lab/M5-TTS-50M-CustomVoice).

## Quickstart

Use Python 3.10 on Linux with a BF16-capable NVIDIA GPU and a compatible CUDA driver. Install from the code repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ASLP-lab/M5-TTS.git
cd M5-TTS
conda create -n m5tts python=3.10 -y
conda activate m5tts
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install --no-build-isolation flash-attn==2.7.3
```

Run from the repository root:

```bash
python infer_clone.py \
  --model ASLP-lab/M5-TTS \
  --text "你好，欢迎使用我们的语音合成模型。" \
  --prompt-wav assets/aslp_default_voice.wav \
  --prompt-text "猪携带该疾病，然后通过蚊子传染给人类。" \
  --output outputs/clone.wav
```

Replace the reference recording and its transcript together to clone another voice. The M5 checkpoint, text tokenizer and [audio tokenizer](https://huggingface.co/ASLP-lab/M5-TTS-Audio-Tokenizer) are downloaded automatically. Use `--lang` for the target language; Cantonese uses `--lang Chinese --accent yue`, and Sichuan uses `--lang Chinese --accent chuan`.

For full usage and evaluation results, see the [project README](https://github.com/ASLP-lab/M5-TTS#quickstart). Only clone voices you own or have permission to use.

## License

Apache-2.0. The Qwen-derived audio codec retains its upstream attribution; see the [third-party notice](https://github.com/ASLP-lab/M5-TTS/blob/main/m5/codec_qwen12hz/NOTICE).

Nodes on GitHub · All samples · Qwen3-ASR for the transcripts · The original model

**[Fish Audio Drama 3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3)**, converted for the native ComfyUI nodes of **[ComfyUI-Drama3](https://github.com/PedroMarinhoDev/ComfyUI-Drama3)**: a 35B text-to-speech model for voice cloning, dialogue and inline cues such as `[sighs]` or `[whispers]`, running **on cards from 8 GB**. 90% of the model is routed experts and each audio frame uses only 8 of the 256 in a layer, so the nodes keep the experts in system RAM and a cache of the ones in use on the GPU. Each file holds the whole model in one file; the codec is separate. Built with Fish Audio. ## Samples No real person is cloned here: the first three clone voices the model made up from a single line, the rest are voices it invents from the prompt alone. Drama 3 FP8, experts in RAM, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.9, top_k 30 (the nodes now default to top_k 0, as Fish Audio's Space does: top_k 30 made some takes fall silent and drop a sentence). **[More on the demo page →](https://pedromarinhodev.github.io/ComfyUI-Drama3/)** **Voice cloning**: the source clip, a voice the model made up from one line, then a new line in that voice > The lighthouse keeper climbed the last step, set her lantern on the sill, and watched the storm roll in across the bay. Somewhere below, a bell began to ring. **Inline cues** > [whispers] Don't move. I think it heard us. [pause] [sighs] Oh, it's only the cat. [laughs] You should have seen your face. **Two speakers** > <|speaker:0|> Did you remember the tickets?
> <|speaker:1|> [laughs] I thought you had them!
> <|speaker:0|> [sighs] Then we're watching the concert from the parking lot. **Five speakers**, no voices given: the model casts all five > <|speaker:0|> [dramatic dungeon master] You enter the dark cave. A dragon sleeps on a pile of gold.
> <|speaker:1|> [brave, too loud] I attack the dragon! … **Singing** > [singing, grand operatic] Oh toast, my golden toast, you're the bread I love the most! [singing softly] Crispy edges, warm and brown, finest slice in all the town. … **Portuguese** > [Brazilian football fan, building tension, Portuguese] Vai, vai, vai, vai! Ele passou por um, passou por dois, [shouting] olha o chute! … ## Files **Start with FP8**: it holds Fish Audio's own expert weights, byte for byte, next to the checkpoint's bf16 layers. The int8 file is the same size, measured as close to the original, and ran 14–17% faster than FP8 on an RTX 3090: the nodes turn FP8 experts into bf16 each time they run, while int8 experts run as int8. Take a smaller file when your system RAM is short of the FP8 file's ~48 GB. Every model file needs the codec. | File | Size | Experts | System RAM | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | [`drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors`](drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 38.6 GB | FP8, as Fish Audio ships them | ~48 GB | the original weights | | [`drama3_int8experts_bf16.safetensors`](drama3_int8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 38.7 GB | int8 ConvRot | ~48 GB | faster than FP8 on the 3090; no silent take in 12 cloned test takes | | [`drama3_w6a8experts_bf16.safetensors`](drama3_w6a8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 32.7 GB | W6A8 | ~40 GB | no silent take in 16 cloned test takes | | [`drama3_w4a8experts_bf16.safetensors`](drama3_w4a8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 24.6 GB | W4A8 | ~32 GB | falls silent more often with real voice clips | | [`drama3_codec.safetensors`](drama3_codec.safetensors) | 1.6 GB | | | the original codec, fp32 | ## Quick start 1. **Install the nodes**: clone [ComfyUI-Drama3](https://github.com/PedroMarinhoDev/ComfyUI-Drama3) into `ComfyUI/custom_nodes` and restart ComfyUI. Nothing to `pip install`. 2. **Download** a model file into `models/diffusion_models` and `drama3_codec.safetensors` into `models/vae`. For transcripts, add `qwen3_asr_1.7b_bf16.safetensors` from [Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI) to `models/asr`, and for the Drama 3 Editor's word-by-word captions, `qwen3_forced_aligner_0.6b_bf16.safetensors` from the same repository. ```bash hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors --local-dir ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI drama3_codec.safetensors --local-dir ComfyUI/models/vae hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI qwen3_asr_1.7b_bf16.safetensors --local-dir ComfyUI/models/asr hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI qwen3_forced_aligner_0.6b_bf16.safetensors --local-dir ComfyUI/models/asr ``` 3. **Open the workflow** `example_workflows/drama3_voice_clone.json` from the pack, pick a few seconds of clean speech, write your text, run. 4. **Edit the take** (optional): the **Drama 3 Editor** node, in place of Decode, shows the take on a timeline with one track per voice and captions that follow the words; it shortens long pauses, spaces out lines that run into each other, flags lines that may have lost words, and cuts. For dialogue, give each speaker a voice: the voice in slot `voiceN` speaks for `<|speaker:N|>`. ## Requirements and speed | | | |---|---| | GPU | NVIDIA, 8 GB of VRAM or more with experts in RAM (tested: RTX 4090 and RTX 3090; 12 GB and 8 GB simulated on the 3090) | | System RAM | the model file plus ~8 GB | | ComfyUI | v0.40 or newer | Drama 3 makes 21.5 audio frames per second of speech, so 46 ms per frame is real time. Experts in RAM, a cloned voice, ~9 s of speech, prompt pass included, measured on 2026-10-15 with an Intel Core i9-14900K (the held rows on 2026-10-14). One frame at a time, decoding waits on the CPU: int8 runs at the same 69 ms per frame on both GPUs, and a CPU with slower cores adds to these times: | GPU | File | Expert cache | ms per frame | |---|---|---|---| | RTX 4090 (PCIe 4.0 ×8) | W4A8 | 16 GB | 52 | | RTX 4090 (PCIe 4.0 ×8) | int8 | 16 GB | 69 | | RTX 3090 (PCIe 4.0 ×8) | int8 | 16 GB | 69 | | RTX 3090 (PCIe 4.0 ×8) | FP8 | 16 GB | 84 | | RTX 3090 held to 12 GB | FP8 | automatic | 137 | | RTX 3090 held to 8 GB | FP8 | automatic | 214 | ## How these files were made From [fishaudio/drama-3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3) with the pack's `tools/convert.py`: - **FP8**: the routed experts' FP8 bytes and 128×128 block scales copied unchanged, gate and up projections fused. - **int8 / W6A8 / W4A8**: the experts dequantized from FP8 in fp32 and requantized, in ComfyUI's comfy_kitchen formats: int8 ConvRot (per-channel int8 after a rotation in groups of 256), or 6-bit or 4-bit codebook weights with int8 activations; relative weight error 0.83%, 2.1% and 7.3%. - **Every file**: the attention, DeltaNet, shared-expert and codebook-decoder layers are the checkpoint's own bf16; the LM head keeps only the rows generation samples from (end of speech and the 4096 semantic codes). - **Codec**: Fish Audio's S2-Pro codec as shipped with Drama 3, weight norm folded in, fp32. Against Fish Audio's own PyTorch code, with the same frames forced, the main token's distribution differs by a KL of 0.004–0.008 nats with the FP8 and int8 files, the noise of bf16 arithmetic. ## License These Fish Audio Materials are licensed under the Fish Audio Community License, Version 1.0.
